a274b22bae.q: What mental framework should a technology leader use to evaluate emerging AI capabilities?
a274b22bae.a: Tobi Lütke spends significant time interviewing new AI models to understand their capabilities, building personal test harnesses called 'evals' — essentially folders of prompts with expected and judged results that he runs against every new model to determine where the edges are and whether the technology has crossed significant thresholds. He compares this approach to how machine learning experts have traditionally worked, using batch jobs that try the same things repeatedly and judge results, similar to how unit tests revolutionized software development in the late 1990s and early 2000s.
a274b22bae.e: How to Live in Everyone Else's Future (with Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke)
f: Build personal test harnesses called 'evals' — structured folders of prompts with expected and judged results — that you run against every new AI model to identify exactly where its capabilities end and what thresholds it has crossed. This approach gives you a repeatable, systematic method to benchmark each model release against your previous tests and determine whether the technology has genuinely advanced.
Building a systematic evaluation framework

Instead of vaguely testing an AI model or relying on marketing claims, create a real testing apparatus. Think of your evals as batch jobs that repeatedly test the same capabilities and judge the results consistently — much like how unit tests transformed software development in the late 1990s and early 2000s.

The premise is simple: write a set of prompts that probe specific capabilities, define what a correct answer looks like, and then run every new model against that same set. This removes guesswork and emotion from evaluation.

As Lütke explains in the podcast , the core insight is that software now exists that no human wrote — and the only way to truly understand it is to interview it systematically. That interview process is your eval framework.

This shift allows rapid iteration and experimentation—though truly critical systems still demand the same careful engineering and oversight they always have.

The economics of software development have fundamentally shifted. Where engineers once had to write production-ready code because iteration was costly, AI-generated code now enables a different approach: ship quickly, test thoroughly, and refine. As Tobi Lütke explains in this episode , this is "extremely healthy" for how companies approach building.
Infrastructure Code and the Speed-Quality Trade-off

Not all code carries the same risk profile. Infrastructure glue—the middleware, connectors, and scaffolding that ties systems together—benefits most from this new rapid-iteration model. Generated code can serve as a credible starting point , reducing the time teams spend on boilerplate and low-risk integration work, freeing human engineers for the deeper problems.

However, this permission to iterate fast does not extend universally. Code that underpins mission-critical functions—payment systems, security boundaries, core logic that directly affects users—still requires the same level of rigor, testing, and intentionality it always did. The shift is not about lowering standards everywhere; it's about redirecting engineering effort toward the systems where human judgment and accountability matter most.
"It is a privilege of a lifetime to be part of another platform shift."

5e2eb14a1e.q: What role should platform abstractions play in software architecture?
5e2eb14a1e.a: Good abstractions should raise the floor — making a minimum quality level accessible — without lowering the ceiling that limits how good something can ultimately become. Lossy abstractions that pretend a system is simpler than it actually is constrain what builders can create on top; operating systems like Windows, Linux, and OS X are examples of abstractions that raise the floor significantly without constraining the ceiling, a property Lütke believes e-commerce platforms should also achieve.

Sorkin's day begins before most people wake. Between 4:30 a.m. and the start of Squawk Box at 6 a.m., he operates in what amounts to a contained edit window: checking email and messages, then making final tweaks and refinements to the DealBook newsletter before it goes out to over one million subscribers. He describes having "the best of both worlds": a television platform that drives newsletter audience and credibility; a newsletter that surfaces stories for deeper book-length investigation; and a summit that generates proprietary interviews and insights flowing back into DealBook.

470cacac8c.q: How should journalists approach sources who have mixed or ulterior motives for sharing information?
470cacac8c.a: Sorkin believes every source has some motivation for talking, and it is typically self-interested. Rather than worrying about their ultimate incentives, he focuses on confirming information from two, three, or four different sources or obtaining documentation. He notes that some of the best sources have completely terrible and ulterior motives—people wanting to screw someone else over, board members trying to stop or advance deals, or bankers who have lost business to competitors and want to leak information.
470cacac8c.e: The Insane Productivity of Andrew Ross Sorkin
f: Accept that every source has some self-interested motivation for talking , and don't waste energy worrying about what it is. Instead, focus on verification: confirm the information from two, three, or four independent sources, or obtain hard documentation. If the facts check out, the motive no longer matters—whether that source is a board member trying to derail a deal, a banker seeking revenge against a competitor, or anyone else with an axe to grind.

As Andrew Sorkin explains in this episode , journalism often happens on the back of sources with the worst possible motives. The insight isn't naive—it's pragmatic. Some of the best investigative stories come from people trying to sabotage someone else or advance their own interests , not from truth-seekers motivated by the public good.

The key is shifting the burden of proof. Don't authenticate the source; authenticate the story. A board member leaking details about a merger to stop it? That leak might be pure sabotage—but if you can cross-check those details with another source, with SEC filings, with email records, the source's toxicity becomes irrelevant. The documentation is what counts.

"I think it's important to understand what their motivation is. But ultimately, as long as I can confirm the information typically from two, three, four different sources, or I can get documentation of the issue, I try not to worry too much about what their ultimate incentives are."

These are junior employees or insiders who lost an auction, were passed over for a major client or deal, or saw years of work stolen by a competitor. With nothing left to protect, they become willing sources.

Sorkin identifies a clear pattern in investigative reporting: great stories begin at very junior levels , not in corner offices. A junior banker who spent months cultivating a client relationship only to watch Goldman Sachs win the account feels betrayed. A business development executive who lost a critical merger to a rival has motive to talk. These individuals are far more inclined to leak information or provide insights to reporters than someone still playing the game and worried about their career.

The mechanism is psychological. When someone has exhausted their options within the system—when they have been rejected, overlooked, or beaten—the only remaining source of control is the ability to upset the situation. For a reporter, this makes them ideal sources. As Sorkin explains in the episode , identifying who has lost something is as important as identifying who has won.

Over 25 years, DealBook has grown to exceed one million subscribers, a result that far outpaced the original projections by a factor of 33.
Launching a business newsletter at the peak of the dot-com bust

DealBook's growth trajectory is all the more remarkable given the timing of its launch. Founded in 2001, Andrew Sorkin launched the newsletter during the dot-com bust , when media companies were pulling back investment and digital business models were highly uncertain. The New York Times' initial estimate of 30,000 subscribers reflected the genuine uncertainty around whether a focused, premium business-news email could sustain itself at all.

What made DealBook different was its specificity and depth. Rather than a broad news digest, it focused narrowly on mergers and acquisitions, corporate deals, and the intersection of business and politics. As Sorkin's work evolved , DealBook expanded to include editorial, video, and the annual Dealbook Summit every December, which has become a flagship forum for business, technology, and political leaders.
From niche email to a media platform

The gap between 30,000 and one million subscribers reveals how much the appetite for specialized business intelligence grew over two decades. DealBook predated Substack by over 15 years and launched before the era of independent newsletter platforms, yet it managed to build a loyal, large audience within the New York Times' institutional structure. This success proved that there was enormous latent demand for curated, expert-driven business coverage—demand that the initial market estimate had simply not anticipated.

Rather than dismiss the teenager as unqualified, the editor saw potential in his knowledge and handed him an assignment. Sorkin seized the opportunity, researching and writing about the technical sounds that modems produced—a topic few readers understood, but one perfectly suited to his natural ability to explain complex technology to a general audience.

This early piece about modem noise was entirely different from the financial journalism Sorkin would later become famous for. Yet it demonstrates how the ability to explain technical subjects clearly shaped his entire career . The assignment proved to be the gateway that transformed his visitor pass into a real position at one of the world's most prestigious newspapers.

f: At age 15, Sorkin created Sports Page Magazine at Scarsdale High School , publishing sports journalism by high school students and distributing it across the country through high schools. He spent roughly a year selling full-page ads at $900 to $1,200 apiece, before the venture collapsed by age 18 due to operational missteps—expensive Federal Express shipping for mailings and severe miscalculations on printing costs with the same printer that produced Wired magazine.

This wasn't just a school project—it was a genuine business model targeting an audience of young male readers through advertising, with circulation happening at a national scale. The operation had real revenue streams and real customers, yet it demonstrated an early lesson that Sorkin would learn before even entering the New York Times at age 18 in 1995: execution and unit economics matter as much as the core idea.

The venture's collapse taught Sorkin a critical lesson about operational discipline that would shape how he approached every project afterward. In the episode, Sorkin reflects on how his early mistakes—underestimating shipping and printing expenses—forced him to understand that even brilliant distribution ideas fail without rigorous cost control.

Federal Express (now FedEx) shipping was a significant operational cost in the mid-1990s for bulk magazine distribution, especially compared to today's digital-first publishing. Sorkin's reliance on this for nationwide distribution of physical copies was one of the core expenses that stretched his margins and contributed to the venture's failure.

What makes this story particularly striking is the contrast with Sorkin's later success. When he launched DealBook in 2001—over a decade before Substack and 15 years before the rise of newsletter culture —he brought these hard-won lessons in cost structure and scalability. That venture, however, succeeded spectacularly: an email newsletter rather than a physical magazine, no Federal Express bills, and ultimately growing to over one million subscribers across 25 years.

4a4a03c557.q: How did Scott Cook's advice influence Zach Perret's decision on the Visa acquisition?
4a4a03c557.a: Scott Cook, founder of Intuit, emailed Zach Perret the day after the Visa acquisition was announced, congratulating him but warning that if the acquisition failed, Perret would be fine and might actually be great. Cook shared that the best thing that happened to him was when Microsoft's acquisition of Intuit was blocked for antitrust, after which Intuit became a multi-hundred billion dollar company. This advice planted a seed in Perret's mind and proved prescient when he decided to walk away from the Visa deal.

f7fb3fbeef.q: What was Plaid's original business model before pivoting to the bank linking API?
f7fb3fbeef.a: Plaid initially built consumer financial products including mobile budgeting tools and spending recommendations, similar to personal financial management tools. The company discovered that nobody wanted to use an app that told them to spend less money. After a conversation with the head of engineering at Venmo, who expressed interest in licensing Plaid's back-end infrastructure, the founders pivoted to focus exclusively on building an API for bank accounts rather than consumer-facing applications.

f61673fc50.q: Were Plaid and Visa direct competitors in the payments market?
f61673fc50.a: Plaid and Visa were not direct competitors. While the DOJ alleged that Visa was a monopolist and that buying Plaid was a path to expand that monopoly, Zach Perret clarifies they did not compete on any specific product. Plaid was building an API for bank account linking and enabling new payment methods, while Visa was the historical credit card payment network. In a meta sense, you could say Plaid represented the new financial system competing against Visa's existing system, but they did not compete on individual products or transactions.
